title: What Happens When a Company Leaves the Stock Market? Understanding Voluntary Delisting
description: Voluntary delisting is when a company removes its shares from public trading on a stock exchange. This means you can no longer easily buy or sell those shares.

faq.q: What happens if I don't participate in the delisting offer?
faq.a: If you don't tender your shares during the offer period, and the delisting is successful, your shares will become unlisted. This means they can no longer be traded on the stock exchange, making them highly illiquid and difficult to sell.

Yes, a delisting offer can fail. This typically happens if the promoters are unable to acquire enough shares to reach the 90% ownership threshold, or if they decide the discovered price through the Reverse Book Building process is too high and reject it.

faq.q: Is the delisting price always higher than the current market price?
faq.a: Not necessarily. While the Reverse Book Building process aims to discover a fair price, there's no guarantee it will be higher than the current market price. It depends on what price shareholders are willing to sell at and what price the promoters are willing to accept.

faq.q: How long does a voluntary delisting process take?
faq.a: The entire process, from board approval to final delisting, can take several months. SEBI regulations prescribe specific timelines for various stages, including public announcements, bidding periods, and settlement.

faq.q: What is the role of SEBI in delisting?
faq.a: SEBI plays a crucial role in protecting investor interests by setting clear regulations for the delisting process. These rules ensure transparency, fair price discovery through Reverse Book Building, and adequate opportunities for public shareholders to exit their investments.
